item.description:
# MILLIMED CO., LTD. (มิลลิเมด) — DATA BREACH DISCLOSURE
**Date Added:** 2026-09-17 **Last Updated:** 2026-09-17 **Country:** Thailand 🇹🇭 **Industry:** Pharmaceutical Manufacturing & Distribution **Website:** millimedthailand.com **Revenue:** ~$70-85M USD (2.5-3.0 billion THB, group annual revenue) **Data Volume:** **~3 TB** (databases, production records, email archives, factory documents, financial data)
---
## Overview
Millimed Co., Ltd. (บริษัท มิลลิเมด จำกัด) is a major Thai pharmaceutical manufacturer headquartered in Bangkok with GMP-certified production facilities in **Samut Prakan** and **Chiang Rai** provinces. The Millimed Group operates through **25+ subsidiary companies** spanning pharmaceutical manufacturing, consumer healthcare brands, supplements, real estate, agriculture, and hospitality.
Their consumer brand **i-HERB**, endorsed by Thai celebrity **Mario Maurer**, is one of the most recognized herbal healthcare brands in Thailand. The company holds **multiple Thai FDA quality awards** and manufactures prescription drugs, OTC products, sterile eye drops (BFS technology), and dietary supplements distributed nationwide through hospitals and pharmacies.
The group's crown jewel subsidiary — **Millimed BFS** — reported **1,423 million THB revenue** and **593 million THB net profit** in 2025, with a staggering **41.7% net margin** and **65% year-over-year growth**. The parent company holds **942 million THB in retained earnings** — they can afford to resolve this.
Millimed's management chose to ignore our communications and failed to protect their data. As a result, we are publishing details of the breach.
---
## What We Have — Over 3 Terabytes
We have obtained **complete access** to the Millimed Group's entire IT infrastructure across **both factory locations and the Bangkok headquarters**. This includes production servers, file servers, NAS systems, ERP databases, email archives, and factory department shares. The total data volume exceeds **3 terabytes**.
### 💊 Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Data (CRITICAL) - **Batch Manufacturing Records (BMR)** for **ALL pharmaceutical products** — the legal backbone of every drug they produce. We hold BMR distribution records from 2016 through August 2026, covering 18+ active product lines including i-HERB, Neoca, Denta Dente, Haelex, Leluxi, Amogin, and more - **Quality Control & Calibration databases** — testing results, equipment calibration records, deviation reports - **Drug Registration & Regulatory Affairs (RA)** data — complete product formulations for Amogin (4 variants), Chlovas, Caltab, BFS eye drops, Lidocaine HCl, Hilazin, Nicardipine, Cystaline-200, Nuosic, and more. **Master Formula documents** included - **Bioequivalence Studies** (Bio Equalise subsidiary) — complete BE study reports, LC-MS/MS chromatography data, OECD compliance documents, and the contract with Chiang Mai University Faculty of Pharmacy - **R&D Department** — pilot batch data, stability studies, cleaning validation, pharmaceutical excipient references (USP 38, BP 2013) - **14 types of GMP audit records** — Thai FDA, Halal, GSDP, GPP, ISO 9001/14001/17025, Pfizer audit, TAISHO audit, iNova audit (including **CAR/PAR corrective action records**) - **i-HERB brand complete IP** — all formulations, BMR, SOP, COA, specifications, cosmetic registrations, and production data for the Mario Maurer-endorsed brand
### 💰 Complete Financial Records (25+ Companies) - **Audited financial statements** (งบการเงิน) for fiscal years **2024, 2025, and 2026** for all major subsidiaries: - Millimed Co., Ltd. — 876M THB revenue, 54M THB net profit - **Millimed BFS — 1,423M THB revenue, 593M THB net profit (41.7% margin!)** - Pros Pharma, MLM Healthcare, Neoca Healthcare, Bio Equalise, i-Herb Innovation, Siriphanwa - **K-Bank and EXIM Bank credit facility summaries** — full loan structures, credit lines, and covenant details - **Monthly sales reports** (January 2025 — **August 2026**) — complete OTC and prescription drug revenue by product, region, sales channel, and individual sales unit - **Oracle ERP database** — every financial transaction across the group. We also have the **Oracle ERP login credentials** (MMNEW/MMNEW@millimed.world) - **Accounting databases** for **all 25+ entities** — complete general ledger, trial balances, tax reconciliation, intercompany transactions - **28 entity accounting folders** with full Chart of Accounts, audit records, tax preparation documents
### 👤 Employee & HR Data (1,000+ People) - **HRM8 database** — complete employee records: names, national ID numbers (เลขบัตรประชาชน), salaries, benefits, performance reviews - **Organization charts** for all 7 production departments (PD1-PD7) with employee names - **Payroll data** for all subsidiaries across three locations - **FingerScan biometric data** backups - **Personal data** of 1,000+ employees across Bangkok, Samut Prakan, and Chiang Rai
### 📧 Email Archives (30+ GB) - **IT Administrator email archives** (15+ PST files) including: - Network configuration and infrastructure credentials - NAS Synology management alerts (neoca-office.synology.me, millimed-office.synology.me) - Microsoft 365 administration - VPN configuration and access management - Vendor communications and support tickets - Backup system notifications
### 🔑 60+ Credentials & Network Access - **Thai Revenue Department (กรมสรรพากร)** login credentials for **ALL 25+ companies** — tax portal access for every entity in the group - **BOI (Board of Investment)** portal credentials — 5 companies with tax incentive access - **Department of Business Development (กรมพัฒนาธุรกิจการค้า)** — 5 corporate filing portal credentials - **Dual VPN access** — WatchGuard Firebox at Ram Intra HQ (210.86.174.42) + **OpenVPN with full certificate chain and private key** for Neoca office (210.86.171.29) - **Oracle ERP credentials** — MMNEW/MMNEW@millimed.world (production system) - **SQL Server logins** including sysadmin (sa), mkuser, DB_ECM, dev_01-03 - **Microsoft 365 tenant** (millimedthailand.com) — cloud email and collaboration - **Active Directory** — domain controller at 192.168.1.2
### 🏭 Complete Factory Infrastructure - **233+ department folders** from the factory file server — every production, quality, regulatory, and administrative department - **22 CCTV cameras + 1 access control** — complete Hikvision surveillance network with IP addresses and serial numbers covering BFS sterile area, laboratories, warehouses, food production, and all manufacturing floors - **31 internal network subnets** (192.168.69.0/24 through 192.168.100.0/24) — full factory network topology - **5 internal servers identified** — AD domain controller, 2x Orion NAS, barcode server, Chiang Rai center NAS - **VMware vSphere** virtualization infrastructure, **CheckMK** monitoring, **Hikvision iVMS-4200** CCTV management
### 🏭 Sales & Operations - **SALES & SALESAPP databases** (12+ GB) — complete sales history, pricing, customer relationships from 2022-2026 - **Monthly sales performance presentations** (January 2025 — August 2026) — OTC + prescription by area, product, channel - **Marketing database** — campaigns, customer targeting, product focus data - **Stock management** — inventory across all facilities - **Forecast data** — business projections and planning - **Transport & logistics** — GPS tracking, delivery records, government pharmaceutical organization reports
---
## Regulatory Impact
Millimed should be aware of the following consequences of this data becoming public:
1. **Thai FDA (อย.) Manufacturing License** — We hold the **actual BMR documents, QA audit records, and 14 types of regulatory audit documentation** including corrections (CAR/PAR). This is not just database records — these are the physical production documents that underpin every drug Millimed manufactures. Release triggers **immediate FDA review and potential suspension of manufacturing licenses**. The FDA Quality Award for 3 consecutive years ends here.
2. **PDPA Violation (พ.ร.บ.คุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล)** — Personal data of **over 1,000 employees** including national ID numbers, salaries, biometric data, and home addresses has been compromised. The PDPA Office can impose fines up to **5 million THB per violation** and criminal penalties including imprisonment.
3. **Revenue Department Exposure** — We hold active login credentials for **ALL 25+ company tax portals** plus the complete intercompany financial structure across the group. The multi-entity accounting data, transfer pricing arrangements, and BOI tax incentive records will be of great interest to Thai tax authorities.
4. **Drug Formulation Theft** — Complete drug formulations including **Master Formula documents**, bioequivalence study data, R&D results, and regulatory submissions for the entire product portfolio. Competitors gain **decades of R&D investment** in seconds. The i-HERB brand formulas, Neoca supplement compositions, BFS sterile manufacturing specifications, and all proprietary pharmaceutical formulations are fully exposed.
5. **Bioequivalence Study Exposure** — Bio Equalise subsidiary's complete BE studies, including the **contract with Chiang Mai University**, LC-MS/MS analytical data, and OECD-compliant study reports. Competitors can use this data to bypass their own bioequivalence testing requirements.
6. **Banking & Credit Exposure** — K-Bank and EXIM Bank credit facility details, loan covenants, and the true financial health of each subsidiary will be publicly available, potentially triggering credit reviews, covenant violations, or credit rating downgrades.
7. **Physical Security Compromise** — The complete **CCTV surveillance network** (22 cameras + access control) with IP addresses and serial numbers, factory network topology, and building plans are exposed. Combined with VPN access credentials, this represents a total physical and digital security failure.
---
## Message to Millimed Management
Chairman **Thongplew Siripornpithak** (ทองเปลว ศิริพรพิทักษ์) and the board of directors had an opportunity to resolve this matter privately. That window is closing.
The data we hold represents the **complete digital footprint** of your 25+ company pharmaceutical empire — **over 3 terabytes** spanning both factory locations, the Bangkok headquarters, and all subsidiary operations. From drug manufacturing records to tax filings, from employee national IDs to bank loan structures, from factory CCTV configurations to Oracle ERP credentials.
Your **Millimed BFS** subsidiary generated **593 million THB in net profit** last year with a 41.7% margin. Your parent company holds **942 million THB in retained earnings**. You can afford to resolve this.
Your **i-HERB brand**, endorsed by Mario Maurer and sold across Thailand, depends on consumer trust. Your **FDA manufacturing licenses** depend on the integrity of your BMR and QA data. Your relationships with **K-Bank and EXIM Bank** depend on financial confidentiality. Your **ISO and Halal certifications** depend on audit documentation security.
**All of this — 3 terabytes of it — is now in our hands.**
We strongly recommend Millimed's management reconsider their position and contact us immediately to resolve this situation before the full dataset is published.
**Screenshots below demonstrate the scope and authenticity of the breach:**
*(See attached: 26 evidence screenshots)*

item.title: [INC RANSOM] Kolin
item.description:
# Kolin Construction
**Kolin Construction** (*Kolin İnşaat Turizm Sanayi ve Ticaret A.Ş.*) is one of Turkey’s major construction and industrial companies. Founded in **1977** and headquartered in **Ankara, Turkey**, the company serves as a flagship business of **Koloğlu Holding**.
## Business Activities
Kolin Construction operates primarily in large-scale construction, infrastructure, and engineering projects. Its areas of expertise include:
* Highways and road infrastructure * Bridges and viaducts * Tunnels * Railways and metro systems * Airports * Ports and marine infrastructure * Dams and hydroelectric power plants * Energy infrastructure * Industrial and mining projects
The company has participated in numerous major infrastructure developments in Turkey and abroad and has regularly appeared in international contractor rankings published by **Engineering News-Record (ENR)**.
## Major Projects
Kolin Construction has been involved in several large-scale and strategically important projects. One of its most notable developments is its participation in the construction of **Istanbul Airport**, one of the largest aviation infrastructure projects in the world.
Beyond transportation infrastructure, the company is active in projects involving power generation, water infrastructure, ports, industrial facilities, and other complex engineering works.
## Other Business Sectors
Through its broader corporate group, Kolin is also involved in several industries outside traditional construction, including:
* Energy and power generation * Mining * Port operations * Shipyards and maritime services * Tourism * Trade and commercial activities
## International Presence
Kolin Construction maintains an international presence and has undertaken projects across **Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa**.
Its international operations have included countries such as:
* Azerbaijan * Libya * Uganda * Poland * Romania * Oman * Saudi Arabia * Kuwait
The company has established representative offices and project operations in several of these markets to support its international engineering and construction activities.
## Company Scale
Kolin Construction is considered one of the prominent Turkish contractors operating internationally. Its annual turnover has been reported in the range of approximately **USD 1.5–2 billion**, reflecting the scale of its infrastructure, energy, and industrial projects.
## Summary
With several decades of experience, Kolin Construction has developed capabilities in managing complex, large-scale infrastructure and engineering projects. Its portfolio covers transportation, energy, industrial construction, and public infrastructure, with operations extending from Turkey to multiple international markets.

[Articles | InfoStealers] Corium: A New ClickFix Panel Shows How Malware Delivery Is Becoming a Turnkey Business
item.description: THREAT RESEARCH / CLICKFIX / CYBERCRIME Corium: A New ClickFix Panel Shows How Malware Delivery Is Becoming a Turnkey Business A newly advertised ClickFix control panel called Corium brings together multiple malware-delivery techniques, deceptive verification pages, website injection, and conversion analytics in a single interface. Its significance lies less in inventing new attack techniques and more in making existing ones easier to manage, distribute, and potentially scale. Corium Appears on Exploit.IN A threat actor operating under the username Cassiopeia has advertised a ClickFix management panel named Corium on the Russian-language cybercrime forum Exploit.IN. The advertisement presents Corium as a platform designed to convert website visitors and advertising traffic into malware executions through deceptive verification workflows. Rather than selling a standalone fake CAPTCHA page, the developer advertises an integrated system covering payload management, landing-page creation, execution methods, campaign analytics, website integration, and notification mechanisms. The screenshots accompanying the advertisement provide a view of the panel’s interface, showing how operators can configure campaigns, upload executable files, select delivery methods, and examine execution statistics. Research assessment: Corium is best understood as a ClickFix distribution and campaign-management platform, not an infostealer family in its own right. The available evidence consists of the developer’s advertisement and screenshots. Hudson Rock has not independently validated the advertised evasion mechanisms, examined a functioning Corium deployment, or attributed a confirmed infection campaign to this panel. Inside the Corium Control Panel One of Corium’s defining characteristics is the consolidation of components that would otherwise require separate infrastructure or tools. The panel is advertised with support for uploaded executables and ZIP archives, customizable landing pages, campaign identifiers, traffic-source tracking, custom domains, and Telegram integration. Its file-management interface allows operators to associate individual payloads with particular delivery campaigns and deceptive page templates. The advertisement also claims that ZIP archives can be automatically extracted. Figure 1: Corium’s file-management interface. The panel displays an uploaded executable named Security.exe and an upload form with options for Windows Update-themed landing pages, campaign names, traffic sources, redirect URLs, custom domains, Telegram chat IDs, and internal notes. The displayed file and run counter do not independently establish successful infections. Source: Corium advertisement on Exploit.IN. This structure reflects an important shift: malware delivery is treated as a managed campaign, with distinct files, landing pages, traffic sources, and reporting configurations. The interface resembles the operational dashboards commonly associated with traffic distribution systems and affiliate marketing platforms, except that the conversion objective is to persuade a visitor to execute attacker-controlled code. Multiple ClickFix Delivery Methods in One Panel Traditional ClickFix attacks frequently rely on a fake CAPTCHA or technical-error page that instructs the visitor to copy and execute a command using a native operating-system utility. Corium expands this approach by advertising several delivery workflows through the same administrative interface. Delivery Method Advertised Behavior Assessment Win + R Uses the Windows Run dialog with headless command execution or in-memory PowerShell variants. Established ClickFix technique. Corium packages several variations. Win + X Uses the Windows system terminal for longer or more complex commands. Variation of existing user-assisted execution tradecraft. Ctrl + L / FileFix Abuses an address bar in Windows Explorer or a browser. Previously documented FileFix technique. search-ms Uses the Windows search protocol to direct a user toward a delivered file. Abuse of an existing Windows capability, not a new primitive. CAPTCHA-triggered download Initiates a file download after interaction with the deceptive verification interface. Another established social-engineering delivery pattern. The developer additionally advertises 14 ready-made Windows DLL-hijacking variations involving trusted system executables, along with portable source code, build instructions, and callback functionality for reporting installations to the panel. The advertisement specifically promotes a headless Windows execution approach associated with conhost.exe , as well as in-memory PowerShell execution. It claims these techniques can reduce visible activity and bypass certain endpoint security warnings. Those security-evasion claims remain unverified. Importantly, none of these mechanisms alone represents a previously unknown exploitation technique. Their significance in Corium is their availability within one configurable operator interface. Figure 2: Corium’s campaign settings display selectable Win+R, Win+X, Ctrl+L, and search-ms delivery methods, alongside Windows Update, Cloudflare, and Windows Defender-themed landing pages. The screenshot also shows visitor links, partner statistics links, and a configurable delivery-command section. Source: Corium advertisement on Exploit.IN. Deceptive Landing Pages Corium advertises several visual templates impersonating familiar security and verification experiences, including: Cloudflare Turnstile verification screens. Windows Update prompts referencing KB5035238. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen-style warnings. Google reCAPTCHA-style verification pages. hCaptcha-style verification pages. The developer claims the templates automatically adapt to different screen resolutions and system light or dark themes. These familiar visual elements can make malicious instructions appear to be part of an ordinary security workflow, increasing the likelihood that an unsuspecting visitor will follow them. Website Integration: An Important Distribution Feature One of Corium’s more operationally significant advertised capabilities is its one-line JavaScript embedding module . According to the advertisement, the system can display a deceptive verification interface over an existing website without requiring the operator to construct a separate landing page. The developer explicitly advertises compatibility with content management systems including WordPress, Joomla, OpenCart, and Bitrix . The interface can display either a CAPTCHA-style modal or a full-screen landing-page overlay. A background-blur option is intended to keep the visitor’s attention on the fake verification prompt. The advertised trigger options include displaying the prompt immediately upon page load, after the visitor’s first click, following a configurable delay, or when the visitor attempts to leave the page. Figure 3: Corium’s website integration module shows a one-line JavaScript embed, selectable CAPTCHA and full-screen overlay modes, configurable activation triggers, background blur, redirect settings, campaign metadata, and Telegram execution-alert templates. Source: Corium advertisement on Exploit.IN. This functionality matters because compromised legitimate websites can become distribution channels for malware, allowing attackers to present malicious instructions to visitors who believe they are interacting with trustworthy pages. A comparable distribution model has already been documented in other ClickFix frameworks. In September 2026, Sekoia published research on Exvicy , another framework advertised on Exploit.IN that used website injection and managed ClickFix delivery. Sekoia identified Exvicy as a copy of the earlier ErrTraffic framework. Consequently, Corium’s JavaScript embedding mechanism should not be described as unprecedented. It demonstrates continued adoption of website injection as a packaged capability in the ClickFix ecosystem. ClickFix as a Conversion Funnel Perhaps the clearest indicator of Corium’s commercialization is its integrated analytics dashboard. The control panel tracks activity across the victim interaction funnel, from initial page exposure to purported payload execution. The screenshot displays metrics for page views, CAPTCHA clicks, executions, conversion rate, and average dwell time . Additional charts visualize executions over time and show browser and operating-system distributions. Figure 4: Corium’s analytics dashboard for Security.exe, showing page views, CAPTCHA clicks, reported executions, conversion rate, average dwell time, runs by day, and browser and operating system distributions. Several metrics are obscured in the screenshot; the remaining charts should not be treated as independent proof of malware infections. Source: Corium advertisement on Exploit.IN. These metrics can help an operator compare different lures and traffic sources, evaluate which techniques produce more execution events, and adjust campaigns accordingly. The advertisement also describes detailed visitor profiles, including operating systems, browsers, countries, languages, screen resolutions, referral sources, and timestamps. Corium additionally advertises partner-facing statistics links, allowing traffic suppliers or other participants to review selected campaign results without receiving administrative access. Telegram notifications are presented as another reporting mechanism, with customizable messages containing variables for the campaign, file, source, browser, operating system, IP address, and event time. Why this matters: ClickFix is increasingly being packaged like performance-driven traffic monetization. Campaign operators can combine deceptive content, selectable delivery paths, referral tracking, and execution reporting in one administrative environment. These features may reduce the operational overhead of running ClickFix campaigns. However, the screenshots do not establish Corium’s customer base, infection volume, distribution scale, or effectiveness. What Is Actually Novel About Corium? Despite its extensive feature list, Corium does not currently appear to introduce a fundamentally new exploitation primitive. ClickFix, FileFix, native Windows utility abuse, deceptive CAPTCHA pages, compromised website injection, and affiliate-style distribution have all been documented before Corium’s advertisement. The potentially distinctive aspect is how comprehensively these capabilities are presented within the same platform. 1. Delivery-Method Consolidation Corium packages multiple user-assisted execution paths into one configurable workflow. This gives operators a broader selection of delivery mechanisms without having to maintain separate tools for each technique. 2. Website-Native Distribution The JavaScript embed module is designed to place deceptive verification content directly over existing websites, combining the credibility of a host page with the attacker’s chosen instructions. 3. Affiliate-Style Campaign Management Traffic-source metadata, campaign names, isolated partner statistics, and conversion analytics suggest a platform designed for repeatable, measurable distribution rather than isolated malicious landing pages. 4. Claimed DLL-Hijacking Toolkit The advertised collection of 14 Windows DLL-hijacking variations is noteworthy as a packaged feature, but the available material does not establish whether these variants are original, reliably functional, or capable of the evasion claimed by the seller. 5. Operational Automation Configurable execution reporting, Telegram notifications, adaptable page layouts, and browser or operating-system segmentation help turn a collection of malicious techniques into a centralized campaign-management product. Several capabilities remain unverified. These include the seller’s claims regarding macOS support, Windows security bypasses, polymorphic payload behavior, and the effectiveness of the advertised anti-detection mechanisms. Overall, the evidence supports describing Corium as a sign of ClickFix commercialization and operational maturity , rather than a technical breakthrough. The Hudson Rock Connection: Monitoring ClickFix Infrastructure Frameworks such as Corium highlight the importance of identifying malicious verification pages and their distribution infrastructure before they lead to successful infections. In July 2026, Hudson Rock introduced a dedicated ClickFix Monitoring capability within its Cavalier Threat Feeds. The module gives security teams visibility into detected ClickFix websites and their associated malicious behavior, including deceptive CAPTCHA interactions and clipboard-based command delivery. Cavalier’s documented ClickFix monitoring data includes: Detected ClickFix websites and domains. CAPTCHA and clipboard-injection indicators. Commands presented to targeted visitors. Before-and-after interaction screenshots. Associated URLs and domain records. Date filtering and intelligence export. Figure 5: Hudson Rock’s Cavalier ClickFix Monitor showing detected ClickFix infrastructure. The system gives defenders visibility into suspicious websites distributing deceptive verification workflows. Source: Hudson Rock, July 2026. Investigating the Payload Behind the CAPTCHA Corium’s configurable delivery methods create a challenge for defenders: different campaigns may expose victims to different instructions or execution mechanisms, even when they are managed through a similar underlying platform. This makes the behavior of the malicious webpage itself an important source of threat intelligence. Cavalier allows analysts to inspect suspicious ClickFix pages, including the commands presented to visitors and visual evidence of the verification workflow. Figure 6: Hudson Rock’s investigation of a ClickFix page hosted on solaric.com.ph. Cavalier presents a suspicious clipboard command together with screenshots before and after interaction with a deceptive CAPTCHA. This is a previously documented ClickFix example, not an attributed Corium campaign. Source: Hudson Rock ClickFix Monitoring research. For Corium-like campaigns, this kind of visibility can be valuable even when defenders have not obtained the operator panel, identified the final malware family, or attributed the activity to a known threat actor. It can support earlier investigation of suspicious URLs, malicious page behavior, and potential user exposure. How Infostealer Infections Can Help Enable ClickFix Distribution The relationship between ClickFix and infostealers is particularly important when attackers distribute malicious content through compromised legitimate websites. One possible entry point is stolen administrative access to a content management system. An infostealer infection can expose credentials belonging to website administrators, developers, or third-party service providers. Attackers may subsequently abuse those credentials to modify websites and inject malicious scripts. This creates a cycle in which an infostealer infection can help enable the distribution of additional malware. Case Study: The Artlist ClickFix Incident Hudson Rock previously documented this connection in a July 2026 investigation involving the digital asset platform Artlist. In that case, attackers compromised a legitimate Artlist subdomain and introduced malicious code that displayed deceptive CAPTCHA content. Hudson Rock and collaborating researcher Matt Kirkland traced the initial access back to an August 2023 infostealer infection involving a freelance developer who had downloaded a pirated Adobe Acrobat installation. The infection exposed privileged WordPress credentials associated with a Senior Content Executive. Those credentials were subsequently linked to the compromise of the website. The attackers injected a malicious script using an EtherHiding mechanism, allowing the compromised website to deliver ClickFix content. The case illustrates how compromised identities and legitimate website infrastructure can intersect in a single malware-distribution operation. Figure 7: The compromised Artlist domain identified in Hudson Rock’s Cavalier ClickFix Threat Feed. Hudson Rock linked the website compromise to credentials exposed through an earlier infostealer infection. The Artlist campaign has not been attributed to Corium. Source: Hudson Rock, July 2026. Corium’s advertised JavaScript embedding capability makes this broader attack pattern relevant. A compromised website with attacker-controlled JavaScript could potentially be used to present a Corium-style verification overlay to visitors. This is an assessment of a plausible distribution model, not evidence that Corium was involved in the Artlist or Solaric incidents. Key intelligence opportunity: Correlating malicious ClickFix websites with exposed CMS credentials and infostealer infections can help security teams investigate not only where malware is being distributed, but also how legitimate websites may have been compromised. Defensive Implications The emergence of more fully featured ClickFix management platforms reinforces the need to monitor the entire distribution chain. Relying exclusively on known malware file hashes or individual malicious commands may provide incomplete visibility into campaigns that can switch landing pages, delivery workflows, and payloads. Security teams should consider several complementary defensive measures: Monitor ClickFix infrastructure: Identify suspicious verification pages, malicious clipboard behavior, and websites displaying unexpected command-execution instructions. Investigate suspicious execution: Correlate browser activity with unexpected launches of PowerShell, Windows command interpreters, terminal utilities, and suspicious use of native Windows protocols. Protect website administration: Monitor CMS changes, unauthorized scripts, third-party dependencies, and suspicious administrator activity. Monitor exposed credentials: Identify compromised WordPress, hosting, and administrative accounts exposed through infostealer infections. Correlate multiple signals: Combine website intelligence, endpoint telemetry, suspicious infrastructure, and credential exposure to investigate the complete attack chain. Educate users: Legitimate CAPTCHA challenges should not require visitors to execute arbitrary terminal commands or install software. Integrating ClickFix Intelligence Through the Cavalier API Hudson Rock also makes the ClickFix intelligence available through Cavalier’s REST API. The documented GET /json/v3/threat-feeds/clickfix endpoint provides access to detected ClickFix sites and associated indicators, while the GET /json/v3/threat-feeds/clickfix/{domain} endpoint supports domain-specific lookups. These feeds can be integrated with existing threat intelligence workflows and security controls, helping organizations investigate suspicious domains and act on known malicious infrastructure. Such monitoring is particularly useful against modular distribution platforms: defenders do not necessarily need advance knowledge of the operator’s chosen malware family to detect suspicious ClickFix delivery behavior. Conclusion: ClickFix Is Becoming More Industrialized Corium provides another example of the continuing commercialization of ClickFix-based malware delivery. Its advertised features combine established social-engineering techniques with a centralized control panel, multiple payload delivery options, embedded website overlays, campaign analytics, and partner reporting. Although the available evidence does not demonstrate a genuinely novel exploit or independently validate the seller’s evasion claims, the platform’s design is operationally significant. It reflects a broader movement toward reusable, configurable malware-distribution infrastructure that can be operated and measured with the sophistication of commercial traffic platforms. For defenders, the challenge extends beyond identifying a particular payload. It involves recognizing malicious user-interaction patterns, identifying compromised websites, and connecting the distribution infrastructure to the credentials and systems that enabled it. Hudson Rock’s ClickFix Monitoring and infostealer intelligence offer complementary visibility into these stages, helping analysts investigate malicious delivery activity and the compromised identities that may sit behind it. Monitor ClickFix Campaigns with Hudson Rock Hudson Rock’s Cavalier platform combines ClickFix infrastructure monitoring, malicious webpage intelligence, and infostealer credential exposure data to help organizations investigate attacker activity. Discover suspicious ClickFix domains, examine deceptive verification pages, investigate exposed administrative credentials, and integrate threat intelligence through the Cavalier API. Explore Hudson Rock Cavalier Sources and Further Reading Exploit.IN: Corium ClickFix Panel advertisement by Cassiopeia, November 2026. Primary source supplied for this investigation. Hudson Rock — Introducing Cavalier’s New Threat Feeds: Deep Dive into ClickFix Monitoring , July 21, 2026. Hudson Rock — How an Infostealer Infection Led to a Sophisticated ClickFix Campaign at Artlist , July 14, 2026. Sekoia — Exvicy: A Copycat of the ErrTraffic Malware Distribution Framework , September 21, 2026. Microsoft Threat Intelligence — Think Before You Click(Fix) , August 2025. Proofpoint — ClickFix Social Engineering Technique Floods the Threat Landscape , November 2024. Huntress — ClickFix Techniques and Variants . Advertised capabilities should not be interpreted as independently verified malware functionality. The Hudson Rock case studies illustrate related ClickFix distribution mechanisms, not confirmed Corium deployments. item.title: [Articles | InfoStealers] Remus Stealer Markets Persistent Gmail Access: Hudson Rock Investigates
item.description: HUDSON ROCK Infostealer Threat Research Threat investigation / Remus Stealer / November 9, 2026 Remus Stealer Markets Persistent Gmail Access: Hudson Rock Investigates Hudson Rock questioned the Remus developer and a person who vouched for its new mailbox feature. Their accounts suggest access established through an infected device. The stronger claim, that newly arriving mail remains readable after account recovery, is still unverified. Original correspondence Mailbox-access claims No Gmail zero-day established Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record. Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions. Hudson Rock examined the version 1.3.9 announcement, contacted the developer, and spoke with a person who publicly endorsed the feature. The resulting correspondence offers a possible explanation for access after the malware exits, but it does not validate the developer’s description of a Gmail “zero-day.” The evidence supports investigating a mailbox-access workflow built into an infostealer service. Its mechanism and claimed resistance to recovery remain unresolved. Visible A mailbox interface Supplied screenshots depict message lists, a verification email, and a Mail action attached to stolen-device records. Source-reported Access after execution The developer describes a process that runs and exits. The customer reports access after browser closure and a password change. Not established Access after full recovery No documented test shows fresh mail being retrieved after effective password, session, and application-access revocation. Figure 1. A Pinterest verification message displayed in the advertised Mail interception interface. This is a supplied screenshot, not a controlled demonstration of live access. 01 / The advertised capability Mailbox access inside the stolen-log panel In the supplied version 1.3.9 announcement , Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the main sales thread advertises that tier at $1,000 per month. The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links. The screenshots present more than an isolated code extractor. They show a webmail-style viewer with senders, subject lines, timestamps, search, and individual messages. Remus’s marketing emphasizes cryptocurrency services and YouTube accounts, but a mailbox may also receive recovery links and verification messages for workplace and other sensitive accounts. Figure 2. A populated inbox view supplied with the reporting material. The interface presents general mailbox contents, not only verification codes. Subscription availability is a vendor claim from the announcement. 02 / Hudson Rock’s direct-source reporting What the developer and customer actually said Asked how the feature operates, the Remus developer pointed to interaction with browser memory and said the software executes and exits. The developer also claimed customers had verified its effectiveness and that the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, while withholding further technical detail. Source Exhibit A. The developer’s description of browser-memory interaction and run-and-exit behavior. These statements describe the operator’s account of the feature. Hudson Rock then questioned a person who had publicly vouched for the service and described using it. In the Russian-language exchange, the source answered yes when asked whether mail remained accessible after a session reset and browser closure. He also said verification messages from different services were available and described seeing messages from the time of what he called the “injection.” Source Exhibit B. The initial customer exchange. The adjacent English text summarizes the relevant answers. English summary / not a verbatim transcript Browser closure and session reset: The source says mail still appears in the panel under those conditions. The exchange does not specify exactly which sessions were reset. Message coverage: He reports receiving codes from different services and seeing messages from the time of the initial “injection.” That term does not identify a verified technical mechanism. Commercial endorsement: He says the feature is worthwhile for his own activity. This is an interested source’s account, not an independent test report. In a follow-up, Hudson Rock asked whether Remus needed to run again at startup or whether one execution was sufficient for later access through the panel. The source leaned toward the second explanation. This was a tentative answer, not technical confirmation of a one-time execution model. Asked separately whether access continued after a Google password change, the source answered that it continued. That short reply is the strongest support in the correspondence for the password-change claim. It supplies no account settings, timing, revocation record, or independently observed result. Source Exhibit C. Follow-up questions about execution and password changes. The source favors one proposed execution model and says mailbox access continues after a password change. View the customer’s panel screenshots in their original conversation context Source Exhibit D. The customer’s submitted inbox and menu screenshots in context. Figures 4 and 5 below reproduce the corresponding standalone images for readability; they are the same evidence, not separate technical confirmations. 03 / Technical assessment The likely explanation is access obtained from an infected device If the source accounts accurately describe the behavior, the leading broad explanation is that Remus acquires or establishes reusable authorization while it has access to a signed-in browser. A remote component could then request mail after the local executable exits, for as long as the service accepts that authorization. This is an inference from the developer’s memory reference and the customer’s account. The material does not identify a particular cookie, token, API, browser-injection method, or account-setting change. The claim of avoiding cookie files also does not exclude using cookies in memory or other browser-held authorization. Access after process exit and access after recovery are different claims. Reusing authorization obtained during an infection could explain why the original stealer need not keep running. It does not, on its own, explain continued access after that authorization has been effectively revoked. Reported condition What it would establish The stealer exits or the browser closes Access may outlive the local process. That alone says nothing about whether the account has been secured or remote authorization invalidated. The password changes The exact recovery action, remaining access paths, and timing matter. A brief source assertion is insufficient to identify what survived. Fresh mail appears after comprehensive recovery A controlled result would support the stronger persistence claim under the recorded test conditions. Identifying a vulnerability would still require technical analysis. Why a stolen-token explanation is not enough Google documents that password changes ordinarily revoke both access and refresh tokens carrying Gmail scopes. Its documented exceptions include Apps Script; existing OAuth-authenticated IMAP connections can continue only for the access token’s validity, usually about an hour. Those details do not establish that Remus uses any of these paths. Google also documents exceptions to being signed out everywhere after a password change. These are reasons to examine the recovery steps precisely, not to assume that any stolen Gmail authorization will remain usable indefinitely. Other explanations remain open: an additional account-access or mail-routing path, incomplete revocation, an unobserved component still operating on the endpoint, or a panel displaying messages collected earlier. None is demonstrated by the supplied material. The developer’s claim that its executable exits does not independently rule out another component or an account-level change. What would establish the stronger claim? A meaningful validation would use an authorized test mailbox and instrumented endpoint, document malware and browser activity, then perform recovery from a separate clean device. Investigators would need a message created and delivered after the recorded password change and revocation steps, followed by evidence of that same message appearing in Remus. The test must account for existing connections, revocation timing, and possible reacquisition of access. The reporting material contains no such controlled sequence, malware analysis, or network telemetry identifying the method. On this evidence, Hudson Rock does not classify the feature as a demonstrated Gmail zero-day. 04 / Supporting panel evidence How the advertised feature fits Remus’s workflow The supplied images place a Mail action beside individual compromised-device records. This integration is the concrete product story: Remus is presenting mailbox reading as another action available while operators assess stolen logs, rather than requiring a separate webmail workflow. Figure 3. The Mail action in the original promotional material. Figure 4. The customer’s log view with the corresponding Mail option, also visible in Source Exhibit D. Figure 5. The customer’s populated inbox screenshot. The sharing control is consistent with the announcement’s advertised mailbox links. The wider dashboards below provide product context. They come from the original promotional material and should not be read as current infection totals or evidence validating the new mail feature. Remus’s broader credential and browser-data theft has also been the subject of earlier technical analysis ; that work predates this announcement. Figure 6. The broader log-search interface. Displayed records and counts are vendor-supplied. Figure 7. An earlier Enterprise statistics view. Its figures are not independently verified victim counts. 05 / Significance and response The risk is easier access to the accounts behind an inbox Stolen authentication material enabling later account access is an established threat, as Google’s discussion of session theft explains. Remus’s run-and-exit claim therefore does not establish a novel technique. The feature is worth examining because it packages mailbox access and advertised sharing inside a commercial stealer panel, while making a much stronger claim about access after recovery. If continuing retrieval of fresh mail is confirmed, an operator could collect new recovery links and verification messages after the initial infection. This could support additional account takeovers, depending on each service’s authentication and recovery controls. The screenshots do not demonstrate a universal MFA bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control of every connected account. Priorities for defenders Isolate the infected endpoint. Preserve relevant evidence and complete remediation before the device is used for trusted account access again. Act promptly from a separate clean device. Change compromised credentials, review signed-in devices, and revoke suspicious sessions and application access. Do not wait for an endpoint rebuild to begin protecting the account. Review the mailbox and recovery settings. Check forwarding, filters, delegation, remote mail access, recovery methods, and recent security activity for unauthorized changes. Investigate dependent accounts. Prioritize services that use the mailbox for sign-in or recovery. Strengthen authentication and recovery controls where supported; a stronger sign-in method does not remove the need to secure an already compromised endpoint. Google’s compromised-account guidance provides the relevant account, device, and mailbox checks. Organizations should also use their identity and endpoint telemetry to establish the scope of exposure. Hudson Rock’s assessment: Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise. The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery. The immediate operational lesson is to investigate the endpoint, account authorization, and mailbox together. A password change is an essential recovery step, but it should not stand in for a review of how access was obtained and what remains exposed. About Hudson Rock Hudson Rock investigates infostealer-driven exposure and helps organizations identify compromised employees and third parties so they can assess and respond to stolen access. Explore Hudson Rock Methodology and scope. This report assesses the supplied Remus sales-thread excerpt and version 1.3.9 announcement, Hudson Rock’s correspondence with the developer and a self-described customer, and the reproduced screenshots. Russian-language answers are summarized in English. The customer’s statements are treated as source claims; the material does not establish the customer’s independence or document controlled test conditions. Screenshots establish what is depicted, not when or how messages were retrieved. This report includes no controlled post-recovery validation or reverse engineering of the new feature. Technical context is linked where used. Assessment dated November 9, 2026. The post Remus Stealer Markets Persistent Gmail Access: Hudson Rock Investigates appeared first on InfoStealers .

item.title: [Articles | InfoStealers] School Bomb Threats: Hudson Rock Finds Reported Sender Accounts in Infostealer Data
item.description: Hudson Rock Research   /   Credential Exposure School Bomb Threats: Hudson Rock Finds Reported Sender Accounts in Infostealer Data Two university email addresses associated with the threats appear in Hudson Rock’s stolen-credential holdings. The Egyptian record dates to a 2021 Vidar infection; the Taiwanese credentials were found in the historical AlienTXTBASE collection. By Hudson Rock November 12, 2026 Investigation & analysis The bomb-threat emails that disrupted Italian schools on November 11 have a significant credential-exposure connection. Hudson Rock identified records for both university email addresses highlighted in threat-related material: f0523219@cloud.dyu.edu.tw and Mosaad_Khalifa@den.kfs.edu.eg . The Egyptian address is associated with a detailed infostealer record containing passwords extracted from an infected computer, including credentials saved against Microsoft authentication pages. Hudson Rock located the Taiwanese credentials in AlienTXTBASE , a credential collection containing aggregated infostealer data. Hudson Rock assesses the matching record as infostealer-derived and dates the reviewed data to more than a year before the threats. Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured. Authentication and mail-delivery records from the providers are needed to determine whether these credentials were used to send the threats. What Hudson Rock found Egyptian university address: a Vidar-associated machine record dated October 1, 2021, with saved Microsoft credentials and a broader collection of browser passwords. Taiwanese university address: a matching Microsoft credential entry in AlienTXTBASE, in data that Hudson Rock dates to more than a year before the threats. The university subsequently reported abnormal bulk sending and suspended the account. The security implication: verified credential theft should trigger containment and closer scrutiny before an account can be repurposed for abuse. The threats that disrupted schools across Europe Reporting published and updated on November 12 followed a wave of threatening emails sent the previous day. ANSA reported that approximately 6,000 Italian schools received the messages , citing the Education Ministry. Some schools evacuated; others continued lessons after consulting police. The recipient count should not be read as an evacuation count. The messages claimed to be from “Mikhail Andropov,” included threats against pupils and staff, and referred to an alleged bomb targeting the prime minister. The name and organizational labels in those emails are claims made by the sender, not verified attribution. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni addressed the disruption on November 11. She said searches had found no bombs and described an attempt to generate fear and chaos. In a video statement reported by ANSA , she said: “We will not allow an anonymous email to decide our children’s school calendar.” Giorgia Meloni, November 11, 2026. Translated from Italian. Figure 1. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s November 11 post on X , shown with the platform’s English translation. Her response underscores the national disruption caused by the threatening emails. The disruption extended beyond Italy. Police in Northern Ireland said more than 300 schools reported the same threatening message. Police Scotland also investigated school threats and assessed them as hoaxes. In Ireland, The Journal reported threats to schools and newsrooms , including its own. It specifically said different addresses were used for the school and media messages. Hudson Rock’s findings here concern the two addresses examined below; they do not establish a common operator or an infostealer connection for every contemporaneous threat. Two university accounts with historical credential exposure Egyptian university address Mosaad_Khalifa@den.kfs.edu.eg Threat connection: the reported address appears in an annotated newspaper screenshot and a public post reviewed in this investigation. Hudson Rock evidence: a Vidar-associated machine profile, system information, and extracted browser credentials. Taiwanese university address f0523219@cloud.dyu.edu.tw Threat connection: independently published by a recipient school; the university reported apparent account compromise. Hudson Rock evidence: a Microsoft URL–login–password entry recovered from the historical AlienTXTBASE collection. The Egyptian account: inside a documented infostealer exposure A photograph used in la Repubblica’s coverage shows the display name “Mosaad Khalifa” and the beginning of a matching email address above the threatening text. The annotated reproduction below identifies the full reported address as Mosaad_Khalifa@den.kfs.edu.eg . Figure 2. Annotated reproduction of la Repubblica’s coverage . The original photograph shows the display name and a partially visible address; the red annotation supplies the full reported address. Select the image to view it at full size. A public post on X also identified that address. An apparent sender address does not establish the identity of the person operating the account, and the legitimate account holder should not be treated as the author of the threats. Figure 3. Public post identifying the reported Egyptian university address. Searching that address in Hudson Rock’s data produced a match to a computer classified in Cavalier as infected with Vidar . The underlying system-information file is dated October 1, 2021 . Figure 4. The Egypt-associated machine in Hudson Rock’s Cavalier platform. A Microsoft authentication entry contains the same university address. Passwords and other sensitive fields are redacted. The interface’s “Unresolved” label is not proof that the password remained usable in 2026. The accompanying browser-password export contains 112 credential records . Twenty use the university email address, including two saved against Microsoft authentication pages. The export identifies Google Chrome as the source browser. 112 Credential records in the reviewed export 20 Records using the university email address 2 Records at Microsoft authentication URLs Recorded infection date October 1, 2021, in the underlying system-information file. Malware classification Vidar, as identified in Hudson Rock’s Cavalier profile. Recorded environment Windows 7 Ultimate, 64-bit; Google Chrome credential export. Microsoft entries login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/authorize ccs.login.microsoftonline.com/ccs/common/oauth2/authorize Additional context System and hardware details, running processes, installed software, and credentials for multiple other services. The saved credentials also show password reuse across services. That broadens the consequences of a single device infection: the same stolen collection can expose several accounts, including a university identity used on unrelated websites. The age of the record is an important part of the finding. It places documented exposure more than five years before these threats. It does not demonstrate five years of continuous attacker access, an unchanged password, or an unremediated infection. What an infostealer takes from a computer An infostealer is malware designed to collect sensitive information from a device and send it to an attacker. Depending on the malware and its configuration, the collection can include browser-saved usernames and passwords, session cookies and authentication tokens, system details, and selected files or cryptocurrency-wallet data. Microsoft’s research describes these capabilities across multiple infostealer families . The Egyptian record makes the process tangible: it combines a description of the computer with passwords stored for services used on it. The Microsoft URLs identify where the browser associated those credentials with a sign-in page. They document exposure of credentials on the endpoint; they do not identify the eventual email-sending system or prove a breach of Microsoft’s infrastructure. If a stolen password remains valid and the account’s controls permit access, someone holding it may be able to sign in later. Session-token theft can create a different route: Microsoft explains that replayed tokens can provide access after the legitimate user has already completed MFA . The files reviewed here do not establish token theft or an MFA bypass in either account. This is why an infection on a computer used for ordinary work can have consequences far beyond that device. A stolen institutional identity can become a vehicle for impersonation, fraud, or disruptive messages to thousands of recipients. The Taiwanese account: credentials exposed more than a year earlier The threat connection for f0523219@cloud.dyu.edu.tw is independently documented. IIS G. A. Remondini, an Italian school that received the message , published the address in its own account of the incident. Focus Taiwan reported on November 12 that Da-Yeh University’s initial investigation found an alumnus account had sent a large volume of email and appeared to have been compromised. The university suspended it, while the cause and the identity of the actual sender remained under investigation. Figure 5. An English-language threatening email bearing the Taiwanese address, with the redacted matching credential entry recovered from AlienTXTBASE added for comparison. The overlay is an analytical annotation, not part of the original email. Hudson Rock found the address in AlienTXTBASE , also known as ALIEN TXTBASE. The matching URL–login–password entry pairs the university address with a Microsoft authentication URL and an exposed password. Hudson Rock assesses this entry as originating from infostealer activity. The collection’s history is well established: Troy Hunt publicly documented its ingestion into Have I Been Pwned in February 2025 . For the specific Taiwanese credential material examined here, Hudson Rock places its age at more than a year before the November 2026 threats . The window for earlier remediation The historical exposure provided a potential warning signal long before the account appeared in bomb-threat reporting. That interval could have allowed exposure monitoring, credential replacement, session revocation, and closer scrutiny of the account’s sign-ins and outbound mail. The university’s later suspension addresses the account’s apparent misuse. The broader prevention opportunity was earlier: identifying the exposed credentials and securing access before abnormal bulk sending began. The age of the data makes timely use of exposure intelligence central to this case. The missing link: from stolen credentials to the sending session The next investigative step is to connect the exposed accounts to the November sending activity. Original emails with full headers can help distinguish an authenticated delivery path from a forged sender or a forwarded message. Provider message traces, sign-in events, and audit records can establish which identity, application, or session submitted the mail. Even successful email-authentication checks do not, on their own, establish that a particular stolen password was used. Could Microsoft and the universities have interrupted the abuse? Verified, unresolved credential theft should trigger an account-security response before further abuse occurs. For identities using Microsoft authentication, Microsoft and the institutions administering those accounts have opportunities to interrupt the chain. The Taiwanese record’s age highlights the time potentially available for that response. Timely action could close a stolen-password access route and help detect subsequent misuse. Microsoft already documents leaked-credential detection in Entra ID Protection . Its service compares discovered credential material with a tenant’s current password hashes and raises a detection when it confirms a match. A historical credential record appearing in Hudson Rock’s holdings does not establish that Microsoft ingested it, that the password still matched, or that an alert was raised. Microsoft also supports risk-based access policies that can require stronger authentication or a secure password reset. The leaked-credential detection and the automated policies are distinct capabilities: sign-in and user-risk policies require the relevant Entra ID P2 or Entra Suite licensing and configuration. A meaningful response to a verified exposure should cover the account, its sessions, and the device: Contain access and replace exposed credentials. Block a compromised account while investigating where appropriate, reset its password through a trusted recovery process, and review any reused credentials. Remove remaining access. Revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens, review app passwords, and remove unauthorized authentication methods, application consent, and mailbox rules. These actions are part of Microsoft’s compromised-account guidance . Remediate the endpoint and strengthen authentication. An infected device can steal replacement secrets. Microsoft’s response guidance includes investigating and remediating affected devices alongside account recovery. Stronger, preferably phishing-resistant authentication helps reduce future password-based abuse. Scrutinize subsequent sign-ins and outgoing mail. New access patterns and sudden bulk sending deserve prompt investigation. Where mail is hosted in Microsoft’s cloud, its outbound protections include sending restrictions and alerts for suspicious sending patterns. A password reset alone is not a complete containment plan. Microsoft notes that revocation timing depends on token and application behavior , and some applications control their own sessions. Nor can an outbound filter be assumed to stop every threatening message before the first delivery. The prevention question is whether actionable exposure intelligence reached the right controls early enough, and whether the affected organizations acted on it. The evidence reviewed here does not establish what Microsoft or either university knew before the threats, which protections were configured, or whether the captured passwords remained valid. Once a provider or institution receives verified evidence of unresolved credential theft, it should investigate promptly, contain affected access, and monitor for abuse. Exposure intelligence becomes protective when it leads to those actions. A stolen account can become a public-safety problem The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft. An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources. Hudson Rock’s contribution is a concrete evidence trail: a documented Vidar exposure for the Egyptian address and a historical Taiwanese credential record in AlienTXTBASE. Connecting that intelligence to account protection gives defenders a chance to secure exposed identities before the next misuse. Acknowledgment: Thank you to International Cyber Digest for bringing this incident to Hudson Rock’s attention. Evidence and methodology This analysis combines public reporting available on November 12, 2026, official police and school statements, five evidence screenshots, the Egyptian machine’s system-information and browser-password exports, and Hudson Rock’s finding concerning the Taiwanese AlienTXTBASE record. The classification and age of that specific record are Hudson Rock’s assessment. Record counts refer to entries in the reviewed Egyptian export, not unique people or verified working accounts. Email capitalization was normalized when matching the reported Egyptian address to the log. Passwords and unrelated account details are not published. No credentials were tested against live services. These findings do not attribute the threats to a particular person, group, or state. Selected sources ANSA: Italian school threats and national response , November 11–12. ANSA: Meloni’s video statement , November 11. Giorgia Meloni: post responding to the school threats , November 11; reproduced in the supplied screenshot. Focus Taiwan: university account associated with the Italian threats , November 12. IIS G. A. Remondini: recipient school’s incident account , November 11. PSNI: threats to more than 300 schools , November 11. Police Scotland: assessment of school threats , November 11. The Journal: Irish school and newsroom threats , November 11. la Repubblica: original photograph and article metadata , November 11. Troy Hunt: ALIEN TXTBASE collection and ingestion into Have I Been Pwned , February 26, 2025. Infostealers.com: analysis of ALIEN TXTBASE’s mixed-source contents , February 26, 2025. Microsoft: infostealer collection capabilities . Microsoft: leaked-credential risk detections . Microsoft: identity-risk controls and licensing . Microsoft: compromised-account response . Microsoft: access revocation and session limitations . Microsoft: outbound sending protections . Microsoft: token theft investigation and response . The post School Bomb Threats: Hudson Rock Finds Reported Sender Accounts in Infostealer Data appeared first on InfoStealers .

item.description: [Professional Services] groupe-alternance.com Groupe Alternance is a French private education group founded in 2008 in Paris, offering work-study (alternance) programs across 5 schools with 10,000 plus students, 300 plus staff and 1,200 plus partner companies. item.title: [HaveIBeenPwned] СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo) - 3,288,711 breached accounts
item.description: In March 2023, data allegedly taken from СберСпасибо (SberSpasibo), the loyalty program of Russian bank Сбербанк (Sberbank), was published online . The data contained records relating to 48M users, including 3.3M unique email addresses alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Data also included bank card numbers stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, plus loyalty program details such as membership dates and the redemption of bonus points for partner offers.

item.title: [HaveIBeenPwned] YouHack - 7,160,849 breached accounts
item.description: In May 2013, the Russian-language hacking forum YouHack suffered a data breach that was later redistributed as part of a larger corpus of data . The breach exposed 107k forum members' email addresses, usernames, IP addresses and MD5 password hashes, most of which were unsalted. Forum posts also contained email address and password pairs belonging to other victims, bringing the total to 7.2M unique email addresses.

item.title: [HaveIBeenPwned] CastleRAT - 179,745 breached accounts
item.description: In November 2026, Europol and international law enforcement partners dismantled infrastructure supporting several malware operations . Among them was CastleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) that enabled criminals to remotely control infected computers. Europol provided HIBP with 180k email addresses associated with CastleRAT infections, along with 893k unique passwords observed more than 3M times across accounts used on infected computers. The passwords are now searchable via Pwned Passwords .
